The verify stage ran five searches (its full budget): they confirmed the Wikipedia titles for Louisa Boren Park and the Carl S. English Jr. gardens (plural in the article title), confirmed Pier 62 exists as a Seattle Parks property but has no dedicated Wikipedia article, and confirmed the Beacon Hill viewpoint's official name (Twelfth Avenue South Viewpoint), location (12th Ave S and S Forest St) and amenities (lawn, two benches; no swing, so that claim was removed). The one reddit query returned no reddit pages, so no reddit-sourced claims are made; a UW IMA green-spaces post and Seattle Parks/official pages that did appear in results are attached as sources where they relate to a spot. All other spots, coordinates, hours and Wikipedia titles were checked against the verifier's own knowledge of Seattle only, conservatively; hours should still be treated as approximate.

spots.name: Kerry Park
spots.blurb: A pocket-sized hillside park on the south slope of Queen Anne with the postcard view: Space Needle, downtown towers, Elliott Bay and, on clear days, Mount Rainier behind it all. People bring a coffee, lean on the wall and watch the light change; it is tiny, so nobody expects silence, but it has a calm everyone-is-here-for-the-same-thing mood. Famous, yes, but still the easiest place in the city to sit and watch Seattle switch its lights on.
spots.tips: Photographers pack the wall at sunset; come at dawn or on a weekday evening, or walk a few blocks west to Marshall Park (Betty Bowen Viewpoint) for a quieter, wider view over the Sound. Street parking only.

safety.note: Residential street with steady foot traffic well into the night; well-lit.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known city park; title and coordinates checked from knowledge only (search budget spent on doubtful spots).

spots.name: Gas Works Park
spots.blurb: A former gasification plant turned grassy headland at the north end of Lake Union, with preserved rusted towers, a big kite hill and a sundial on top. Locals sprawl on the slope facing downtown, watch seaplanes land and kayaks drift, and stay through sunset as the skyline lights up across the water. Big enough that even on a busy day you can find your own patch of grass.
spots.tips: Head up Kite Hill for the widest view, or drop down to the concrete steps at the water's edge for a quieter perch. Wind off the lake gets chilly after sundown, so bring a layer; summer weekends and July 4 are the only truly crowded times.

spots.name: Discovery Park South Bluff
spots.blurb: Seattle's largest park is 534 acres of meadow, madrona forest and bluff on the old Fort Lawton grounds, and the South Bluff is where the Loop Trail opens onto a wide grassy edge above Puget Sound with the Olympics across the water. It is far enough from the parking lots that it stays hushed even on weekends; people sit in the tall grass, read, or watch ferries and container ships crawl past. In the evening the sun drops straight into the Olympics.
spots.tips: Park at the South Lot off W Emerson St and follow the Loop Trail west for about 15 minutes; there are only a couple of benches, so bring a blanket. Continue down to West Point Lighthouse if you want driftwood and beach instead of meadow.

safety.note: Trails are unlit and the park is huge; plan to be back at the lot by dusk and stay on the marked Loop Trail (the bluff edge is fenced only in places).

spots.verifyNote: Park and article title well established; South Bluff coordinates are an estimate along the Loop Trail.

spots.name: Kubota Garden
spots.blurb: Twenty acres of Japanese-style garden built over decades by Fujitaro Kubota and his family in south Seattle, now a free city park that many people north of I-90 have never visited. Stone bridges, koi ponds, mossy paths and a hillside 'mountainside' with waterfalls, all tucked into a residential neighborhood. It is genuinely quiet: you hear water and birds more than people.
spots.tips: The Moon Bridge and the overlook above the Necklace of Ponds are the classic sit-and-stare spots; weekday mornings are near-empty. No food service and few benches deep in the garden, so bring water; Link light rail to Rainier Beach plus a 15-minute walk gets you there.

sources.label: UW IMA: exploring green spaces (Kubota Garden as a quiet spot)

safety.note: Calm and family-friendly; the garden has no lighting, so treat it as a daylight spot.

spots.name: Seattle Central Library
spots.blurb: Rem Koolhaas's glass-and-steel diamond downtown is the city's best free indoor hang: the Level 10 Reading Room sits under the slanted glass roof with views toward Elliott Bay and the downtown grid, and the Level 3 'Living Room' is a bright atrium where you can read a magazine all afternoon. Nobody checks whether you are actually working. On rainy days it fills with people doing exactly that.
spots.tips: Take the elevator straight to Level 10 for the quietest tables and the view, then walk down the Books Spiral on Levels 6-9. Weekend afternoons fill up; weekday mornings are calm. Free wifi and outlets at most tables.

safety.note: Staffed with security on site; busy downtown block, fine into the evening.

spots.verifyNote: Landmark library; title and coordinates checked from knowledge only. Trimmed one hyperbolic line.

spots.name: Frye Art Museum
spots.blurb: A small, always-free art museum on First Hill built around a founding collection of moody 19th-century German and American paintings, with rotating contemporary shows. It is rarely crowded, the galleries are hushed and softly lit, and there is a bright cafe and a reflecting pool by the entrance. Locals treat it as the place to lose an hour when it rains.
spots.tips: Admission and the small lot on Terry Ave are both free, which is rare this close to downtown. The salon-style hang of the founding collection is the best room to sit in; the cafe is a solid quiet lunch stop too.

safety.note: Quiet hospital district; fine during opening hours.

spots.verifyNote: Long-established free museum; title and coordinates checked from knowledge only.

spots.name: Elliott Bay Book Company
spots.blurb: Seattle's big independent bookstore, relocated from Pioneer Square to a converted warehouse on 10th Ave with cedar shelves, skylights and creaky wood floors. Reading nooks are scattered through the store, and Little Oddfellows cafe at the back serves coffee and small plates to people who have clearly been there for hours. Nobody hurries you out.
spots.tips: The cafe tables at the back and the chairs on the mezzanine are the calm corners; Capitol Hill weekends get busy, so go on a weekday. Author readings happen most evenings, which is either a bonus or a reason to come earlier.

safety.note: Busy Pike/Pine block, well-lit and active into the evening.

spots.verifyNote: Title and coordinates checked from knowledge only; hours approximate.

spots.name: Louisa Boren Park
spots.blurb: A 7-acre wooded hillside and lookout at the north end of Capitol Hill, carved out of Interlaken Park in 1913 and sitting just northeast of Volunteer Park, that almost nobody outside the neighborhood knows about. From the bench you look northeast across Lake Washington to the Eastside and the Cascades, so it catches sunrise light the west-facing famous viewpoints never see. Mostly dog walkers and one or two people with coffee.
spots.tips: Enter from 15th Ave E at E Garfield St; the benches near the top are the spot, and the rest of the park drops steeply into Interlaken's forest trails. Bring a thermos: there is nothing nearby but houses.

safety.note: The overlook is fine at dawn and in daylight; the wooded trails below are unlit and isolated, so skip them after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Wikipedia title confirmed by search; Seattle Parks lists it as 'Boren Park'. Blurb aligned to the article (7.2 acres, views NE over Lake Washington).

spots.name: Seward Park
spots.blurb: A 300-acre peninsula of old-growth forest jutting into Lake Washington with a flat 2.4-mile paved loop around the shoreline. The east side faces the lake and the Cascades, so early mornings bring a still lake, mist and the sun rising over the mountains, with Mount Rainier showing to the south on clear days. The loop is popular with runners, but the pebble beaches and grassy points just off it are quiet.
spots.tips: Walk the loop counter-clockwise so the sunrise is in front of you; the north tip and the small beaches on the east shore have the best places to sit. The entrance lot fills on summer weekends, so come early.

safety.note: The loop is busy with walkers from dawn; interior forest trails are unlit, so stick to the shoreline at dusk.

spots.verifyNote: Major city park; title and coordinates checked from knowledge only.

spots.name: Pier 62
spots.blurb: The rebuilt one-acre public pier on the downtown waterfront, reopened in 2020 as the first piece of the new Waterfront Park: a wide open deck over Elliott Bay with benches, a floating dock and nothing to buy. Ferries slide in and out of Colman Dock, the Olympics sit across the water, and after dark the pier is lit and the promenade stays busy enough to feel easy. It is the closest thing downtown has to a place where you just sit and look west.
spots.tips: The benches on the west edge get the sunset; the floating dock on the north side is the quietest corner. The Overlook Walk behind the pier climbs to Pike Place Market if you want a second viewpoint. Check the Friends of Waterfront Park calendar, since concerts and events sometimes take over the deck.

sources.label: Friends of Waterfront Park: Visit Pier 62

safety.note: Well-lit waterfront with park staff and steady foot traffic in the evening; closes at 10pm.

spots.name: Olympic Sculpture Park
spots.blurb: The Seattle Art Museum's free outdoor sculpture park zigzags from Belltown down to the water, with Calder's red 'Eagle' framing the Space Needle and a small pocket beach at the bottom. People come to lie on the lawn and watch ferries rather than study art, and the path keeps going north into Myrtle Edwards Park, a long bench-lined shoreline that is even quieter.
spots.tips: The lower lawn by the beach and the benches along the Myrtle Edwards trail are the calm spots; the upper pavilion plaza is busiest. Sunset lands directly across the Sound on the Olympics; bring a jacket for the wind off the water.
spots.hours: 30 min before sunrise to 30 min after sunset

safety.note: Open and populated until dusk; the park closes shortly after sunset.

spots.name: Carl S. English Jr. Botanical Garden
spots.blurb: Seven acres of botanical garden on the grounds of the Ballard Locks, planted over 43 years by the Army Corps gardener it is named after, with more than 500 species and a wide lawn sloping toward the ship canal. Most visitors walk straight through to watch boats in the locks; if you stop under the trees it is one of the quietest lawns in the city, with the spillway murmuring in the background.
spots.tips: Enter through the main Locks gate on NW 54th St; the lawn on the west side of the garden and the benches above the canal are the picnic spots. Salmon run at the fish ladder in summer and early fall, which is when weekends get busy.

spots.name: Twelfth Avenue South Viewpoint
spots.blurb: A one-acre strip of lawn with two benches on the western bluff of North Beacon Hill, with a straight-on view of the downtown skyline, the stadiums, Elliott Bay and the port cranes below, and the Olympics beyond. It is the kind of place you learn about from a friend: used almost only by neighbors and the occasional photographer, a few people at sunset, someone on a bench after dark watching the towers light up. No facilities, no crowd, just the view.
spots.tips: Find it at 12th Ave S and S Forest St (2821 12th Ave S); street parking on 12th, or about a 10-minute walk from Beacon Hill Link station. Go at blue hour for the skyline lights; there are only two benches, so bring a blanket for the grass.

sources.label: Seattle Parks: Twelfth Avenue South Viewpoint

safety.note: Quiet residential street with streetlights but little foot traffic late; fine at dusk, go with a friend if you stay past 10pm.

spots.verifyNote: Confirmed as a Seattle Parks property; renamed to the official name, cross street corrected from S McClellan to S Forest St, and the unverified swing removed (park has a lawn and two benches). No Wikipedia article.

spots.name: Alki Beach
spots.blurb: A 2.5-mile sandy beach and promenade in West Seattle with the downtown skyline across Elliott Bay and the Olympics to the west. Locals walk or bike the path, sit on driftwood logs, and in summer light fires in the beach fire pits after sunset. It is well used and well lit, so it works as a night spot when most Seattle parks feel empty.
spots.tips: The stretch near the Alki Bathhouse (60th Ave SW) has the fire pits and most of the life; walk east toward Duwamish Head for the best skyline view and fewer people. Fire pits are first-come and busy on summer weekends; bring your own wood.

safety.note: Lit promenade with regular foot and bike traffic; summer weekend nights get loud with cruising car traffic on Alki Ave SW, so the beach side of the path is the calmer place to sit.
